sounds.intro: Swedish is written in the Latin alphabet with three extra letters at the end: å, ä, ö. Nouns are "en" or "ett" words. The language has a sing-song pitch, and long and short vowels matter.
rows: say "ur" with rounded lips, like "ur" in "fur"
say "ee" with rounded lips, like German "ü"
a rounded "ew", like a short "oo" said with the lips forward
a hushing sound, between English "sh" and German "ch"
tj / k (before e, i, y, ä, ö)
"y", as in "yes", before e, i, y, ä, ö
notes: Double consonants make the vowel before them short. A single consonant after a stressed vowel means the vowel is long.

grammar.title: Pronouns
text: Swedish always uses the pronoun. "Du" is you, "ni" is the polite or plural you. "Han" is he, "hon" is she, "det" or "den" is it.

grammar.title: Singular and plural
text: Nouns are "en" words or "ett" words. There are five plural endings: -ar, -or, -er, -n, or no ending. Learn the plural with each noun.

grammar.title: To be: vara
text: "Vara" (to be) has one form for everyone in the present: är.

grammar.title: Ha: have
text: "Att ha" (to have) is "har" in the present for everyone. "Det finns" means "there is".

grammar.title: Present tense
text: Take the stem and add -ar, -er or -r. Arbeta (to work): jag arbetar. The ending is the same for every person.

grammar.title: Basic sentences
text: The verb is always the second item: Jag läser en bok. If another word comes first, the verb still stays second: Idag läser jag en bok.

grammar.title: Negation
text: Put "inte" after the verb: Jag går inte. In questions and with a second verb, "inte" comes after the subject.
ex: I do not have a car
he does not work on Sundays

grammar.title: Asking questions
text: Put the verb first: Är du student? A question word goes before the verb: Var bor du?

grammar.title: Question words
text: A question word comes first, then the verb.

grammar.title: Possessives and liking
text: The word agrees with the noun: min / mitt / mina (my), din / ditt / dina (your), hans, hennes, vår / vårt / våra (our), er / ert / era (your, formal), deras (their). To like something, use "gilla".

grammar.title: Formal vs informal
text: Swedish almost always uses "du", even with strangers and older people. "Ni" is rare and can sound stiff. Use "du" unless you are sure.
rows: hur mår du? / hur mår ni?
hewr MOHR dew / hewr MOHR nee

grammar.title: Past and future (simple)
text: Past: add -ade, -de, -te, or a changed stem. Jag arbetade (I worked), jag gick (I went). Future: "ska" or "kommer att" + verb.

grammar.title: Commands
text: Informal: the bare stem (kom). Formal: the same, with "tack" to be polite. To forbid, use "inte" or "ingen".

grammar.title: Can, must, want
text: Kunna (can): jag kan. Måste (must): jag måste. Vilja (want): jag vill. The second verb stays in its basic form.
ex: I do not want to eat

grammar.title: In, on, at
text: Common words: i (in), på (on, at), vid (at, by), till (to), från (from), med (with), under (under).
ex: the book is on the table
the cat is under the table
the shop is next to the bank
the park is near the station
the key is in the bag

grammar.title: Comparing things
text: Add -are for "more", -ast for "the most": stor, större, störst (irregular). Many adjectives: snabb, snabbare, snabbast. "Than" is "än".
ex: det här är bättre än det där
deh hair air BET-treh en deh dair
det här är sämre än det där
deh hair air SEM-reh en deh dair
